note: Content source for the Practice page — exercises the Coach derives from the week's brief. Split out of Control-Hub.json, where it was a tab called 'Backlog'; that name read as a to-do list of my own work, which is the opposite of what it is. Every exercise carries `fromBrief` naming the news item it came from, because the derivation is the entire point and was invisible before. `nav` carries exact relative hrefs from application/ — do not infer paths. Today the page is generated in Claude Design from this file; there is no build script in this repo.

site.title: Reading, turned into building
site.lede: Not a to-do list of my work. These are exercises the Coach generates from whatever showed up in the week's brief — each one traced back to the item that prompted it, sized to about an hour, and grounded in a repository I already own.
site.actNote: Skippable by design. Nothing expires and there is no weekly streak to maintain — a backlog that generates guilt is the problem I was trying to solve, not a feature.

how.title: How an exercise gets here

steps.label: Something lands in the brief
steps.body: A spec change, a paper, a release — anything the Framer thought was worth my attention.

steps.label: The Coach asks what I'd have to build to understand it
steps.body: Not to summarise it again. The test is whether I could implement the idea, not restate it.

steps.label: It lands here, sized to an hour
steps.body: Scoped to one working session with setup excluded, and pointed at a repository I already have.

how.footnote: Skippable by design. Nothing expires and there is no weekly streak to maintain — a backlog that generates guilt is the problem I was trying to solve, not a feature.

exercises.title: Have Claude Code build a minimal stateless 'echo' MCP server

fromBrief.label: From: MCP's 2026-07-28 spec moves the core from stateful to stateless

exercises.goal: Feel the stateless model firsthand — one 'echo' tool, no session state, any instance able to answer.
steps: Ask Claude Code for a minimal MCP server with a single 'echo' tool on the 2026-07-28 stateless spec
Have it comment the places where session state would have lived under the old model
Run it, call the tool twice, and confirm no session was needed between calls
exercises.note: Queued after the first one. This is the exercise that makes the lineage obvious — the brief item is the reason it exists.

priorArt.label: No prior art
priorArt.detail: No MCP server implementation found in any connected repository.

shipped.title: Already shipped
shipped.body: Completed work, kept so the page shows progress rather than only obligation.

items.text: Created the GitHub repo for the project — description, Python .gitignore, licence decided later.
Cloned locally and got credential auth working through the system keychain.
Installed the Claude Code CLI, fixed the PATH, and ran the first live session.

wip.title: The Coach that writes these isn't built yet
wip.body: The two exercises above are hand-written examples in the shape the Coach will produce. The agent that reads a week of briefs, picks the concept worth an hour, and grounds it in a repository you already own is designed and specified, not written — it arrives in a later phase. What it will be graded on is whether the module it names actually exists, plus whether the exercises get completed and how long they really take.
wip.linkLabel: See where it sits in the plan

footer.note: Practice renders data/state/backlog.json. Sample data until the Coach is built.

reconciliation.title: Before an exercise is offered, check whether I already built it
reconciliation.body: The Coach has read access to my repositories for one reason already: confirming the module an exercise targets actually exists. The same access answers a second, more useful question — have I already done this? An exercise for something sitting finished in a repo is worse than no exercise; it is the fastest way for a recommender to lose trust.

states.label: No prior art
states.body: Nothing related found. Offer the exercise as written.

states.label: Partly there
states.body: Related code exists. Offer a narrowed version that starts from what is already built rather than from zero.

states.label: Already built
states.body: A working implementation exists. Retire the exercise and say where the code is, so the answer is a pointer rather than busywork.

reconciliation.biasNote: Deliberately recall-biased, for the same reason the Gatekeeper is. A wrong already built silently withholds an exercise I never learn existed — invisible, and the exact failure this whole system was built to avoid. A wrong no prior art merely wastes a few minutes and is self-correcting the moment I open the repo. When the check is unsure it offers the exercise with a note, never suppresses it.

flywheel.title: Why Practice is the most valuable signal in the system
flywheel.lede: Rating a brief item tells the system what I said was interesting. Finishing an exercise tells it what I actually spent an hour on. The second is worth far more, and it is the only place this system gets it.

steps.label: An item lands in the brief
steps.body: The Framer decided it was worth my attention today.

steps.label: The Coach turns it into an hour of work
steps.body: Scoped to a repo I own, after checking I have not already built it.

steps.label: I finish it, skip it, or overrun
steps.body: Nobody is asked to rate anything. The behaviour is the rating.

steps.label: The Tuner reads the behaviour
steps.body: Completion adjusts what the Framer surfaces; overrun adjusts how the Coach sizes an hour; the skip reason decides which of the two is wrong.

steps.label: Tomorrow's brief is better
steps.body: Not because I graded it, but because I built something.

head: Signal
What it means
Feeds
rows: The strongest evidence a brief item mattered — stronger than any rating, because it cost me an hour
The Framer surfaced something I do not care about
The topic was right; the Coach mis-sized it
Calibration. An hour that takes three is a scoping failure, not a me failure
The long-horizon signal — did the exercise leave anything behind
The reconciliation check misjudged what I had already built

twoAxes.title: The same split as everywhere else: what is checkable, and what is taste
rows: Does the module the exercise names exist? Was the prior-art verdict correct? Both are answerable against the repository with no opinion involved, so both can block.
Was this worth an hour? Only I can answer, only over many weeks, and never from a single data point. Reported, never a gate.

guardrail.label: The obvious way to break this
guardrail.body: If the Tuner optimises for completion rate, the Coach learns to generate trivial exercises — completion goes up, the product gets worse, and the metric reports success the entire time. So completion rate is a diagnostic, never a target. It is only read alongside actual-versus-estimated time and whether the code was reused: an exercise finished in ten minutes and never touched again is a failure that a completion count would score as a win.

diagram.caption: Each turn leaves the next one better informed. The loop is the product — a single exercise is just an exercise.

flywheel._render: Render `diagram.svg` as the flywheel. Do NOT lay the five steps out as tiles or a row of cards with a 'back to step 1' link — that is a list with a footnote, not a loop. The steps[] array is retained only as the accessible text alternative and for narrow screens where the circle cannot be read.

zones._why: This page serves two different visits and was treating them identically. Returning to DO work (find the exercise, mark it done) is a different task from arriving to UNDERSTAND the system. Undifferentiated, the actionable 20% was buried in the explanatory 80%. Three zones, three visual registers, act first.

act.title: Open exercises
act.subtitle: One on the bench. Skippable — nothing expires.
act.design: The work surface. Raised panels with visible elevation, the warm panel tone against the page background, terracotta accents, strong serif titles. Everything interactive lives here and should look interactive: status chips with hover and press states, a clear cursor change. Highest contrast on the page. This zone comes FIRST, immediately after the hero — a returning reader should never scroll past explanation to reach their work.

understand.title: The mechanism behind the list
understand.subtitle: Nothing to do here — this is the reasoning, for anyone who wants it.
understand.design: Reading matter, not a work surface. Flat — no elevation, no card borders, sitting directly on a cooler recessed background tone so the zone change is felt before it is read. Narrower measure for reading. Muted labels, no interactive affordances whatsoever, so nothing here invites a click that does nothing. Where a block carries a 'Designed, not built' chip, that chip belongs in this register too.

record.title: Shipped
record.subtitle: Finished, or retired before it reached the bench.
record.design: Quietest of the three. A dense dated list, small type, low contrast — an archive rather than a feature. It should be the last thing that draws the eye.

zones.divider: Between zones, a full-width rule with the next zone's eyebrow set in small letterspaced monospace. The transition from act to understand is the important one: after it, nothing asks anything of the reader.

retired.title: Retired before I saw them
retired.body: Exercises the prior-art check found I had already built. They are kept visible rather than deleted — a retired exercise is the check working, and silently dropping it would hide the one piece of evidence that it runs at all.

items.title: Set up the project repo using the Claude Code CLI

fromBrief.label: Prompted by the CLI tooling thread in the brief

items.goal: End with a new GitHub repo, Claude Code running against it, and one commit the agent made for you.
steps: Create an empty GitHub repo and clone it locally
Install and authenticate the Claude Code CLI
Have it scaffold the project structure and make the first commit
Read the diff before approving it — the point is reviewing agent output, not accepting it
items.note: First CLI session. Deliberately unambitious: the goal is the workflow, not the code.

priorArt.label: Already built
priorArt.detail: This repo exists and the CLI is in daily use — the check would retire this one and point at the commit history instead.

retired.label: Retired — already built
retired.reason: This repo exists and the Claude Code CLI is in daily use. The exercise was already done before it was offered.

statusRule: A status and a prior-art verdict are never shown together. none and partial leave the exercise active and it carries a status; built is terminal — it retires the exercise, removes the status entirely, and returns a pointer to the code instead. An exercise showing both In progress and Already built is a contradiction, not two facts.
